# Local stack. No .env file required — every value here is either a
# throwaway dev credential (never used anywhere but this compose network)
# or a placeholder that's safe to commit. Real secrets live in the deploy
# target's secret store, never here.
#
# db (owner) -> migrate (owner, DDL/grants) -> seed (owner, fixture data)
#            -> portal / notifier (least-privilege app roles)

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:18-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
      POSTGRES_DB: wellis
    ports:
      # Loopback only — this used to be 0.0.0.0, reachable from anywhere
      # (see FINDINGS.md SEC-03). A GUI on the same machine can still
      # reach it on 127.0.0.1:5432.
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
    volumes:
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql/data
      # Local-only: creates portal_app/notifier_app. Only runs once, on
      # first init of an empty data dir. See db/init/01_roles.sql.
      - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres -d wellis"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s

  # One-shot: applies migrations/*.sql (including the role grants) as the
  # owner, then exits. Nothing else starts until this succeeds.
  migrate:
    image: postgres:18-alpine
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    volumes:
      - ./migrations:/migrations:ro
      - ./scripts:/scripts:ro
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis
    entrypoint: ["sh", "/scripts/migrate.sh"]

  # One-shot: loads the synthetic demo data (skips itself if already
  # loaded). Runs as the owner — it inserts into patients, which the app
  # roles can't (they're read-only there by design).
  seed:
    build: ./notifier
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    volumes:
      - ./scripts:/scripts:ro
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis
    entrypoint: ["python", "/scripts/seed_db.py"]

  portal:
    build: ./portal
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      seed:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis
      PORT: 8080
      # Fixed LOCAL-ONLY dev token, not a secret: raw value is
      # "[REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN]" (see README's curl example). name:sha256hex —
      # see portal/src/auth.js.
      API_TOKENS: "local:[REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN_SHA256]"
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "--no-verbose", "--tries=1", "--spider", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s

  notifier:
    build: ./notifier
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis
      # Empty -> dry-run: logs what it would send and marks reminders
      # sent, instead of calling a real provider. We have no real
      # provider locally (or, currently, at all).
      MESSAGING_URL: ""
      MESSAGING_KEY: ""
      # Unset -> no receipts written. No default bucket, on purpose.
      RECEIPT_BUCKET: ""
    # The image's own CMD is the Lambda handler entrypoint, which expects
    # the Lambda Runtime API and just hangs locally. Override it to run
    # the polling loop instead.
    entrypoint: ["python", "notifier.py"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "sh", "-c", "tr '\\0' ' ' < /proc/1/cmdline | grep -q notifier.py"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s

volumes:
  pgdata:

lines: +      # postgres:18+ images store data under /var/lib/postgresql itself
# Local-only: creates portal_app/notifier_app. Only runs once, on
# first init of an empty data dir. See db/init/01_roles.sql.

# Local stack. No .env file required — every value here is either a
# throwaway dev credential (never used anywhere but this compose network)
# or a placeholder that's safe to commit. Real secrets live in the deploy
# target's secret store, never here.
#
# db (owner) -> migrate (owner, DDL/grants) -> seed (owner, fixture data)
#            -> portal / notifier (least-privilege app roles)

services:
  db:
    image: postgres:18-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: postgres
      POSTGRES_DB: wellis
    ports:
      # Loopback only — this used to be 0.0.0.0, reachable from anywhere
      # (see FINDINGS.md SEC-03). A GUI on the same machine can still
      # reach it on 127.0.0.1:5432.
      - "127.0.0.1:5432:5432"
    volumes:
      # postgres:18+ images store data under /var/lib/postgresql itself
      # (versioned subdirectory), not .../data — see
      # https://github.com/docker-library/postgres/pull/1259
      - pgdata:/var/lib/postgresql
      # Local-only: creates portal_app/notifier_app. Only runs once, on
      # first init of an empty data dir. See db/init/01_roles.sql.
      - ./db/init:/docker-entrypoint-initdb.d:ro
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U postgres -d wellis"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 10
      start_period: 5s

  # One-shot: applies migrations/*.sql (including the role grants) as the
  # owner, then exits. Nothing else starts until this succeeds.
  migrate:
    image: postgres:18-alpine
    depends_on:
      db:
        condition: service_healthy
    volumes:
      - ./migrations:/migrations:ro
      - ./scripts:/scripts:ro
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis
    entrypoint: ["sh", "/scripts/migrate.sh"]

  # One-shot: loads the synthetic demo data (skips itself if already
  # loaded). Runs as the owner — it inserts into patients, which the app
  # roles can't (they're read-only there by design).
  seed:
    build: ./notifier
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    volumes:
      - ./scripts:/scripts:ro
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis
    entrypoint: ["python", "/scripts/seed_db.py"]

  portal:
    build: ./portal
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
      seed:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis
      PORT: 8080
      # Fixed LOCAL-ONLY dev token, not a secret: raw value is
      # "[REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN]" (see README's curl example). name:sha256hex —
      # see portal/src/auth.js.
      API_TOKENS: "local:[REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN_SHA256]"
    ports:
      - "127.0.0.1:8080:8080"
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "wget", "--no-verbose", "--tries=1", "--spider", "http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 5
      start_period: 5s

  notifier:
    build: ./notifier
    depends_on:
      migrate:
        condition: service_completed_successfully
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis
      # Empty -> dry-run: logs what it would send and marks reminders
      # sent, instead of calling a real provider. We have no real
      # provider locally (or, currently, at all).
      MESSAGING_URL: ""
      MESSAGING_KEY: ""
      # Unset -> no receipts written. No default bucket, on purpose.
      RECEIPT_BUCKET: ""
    # The image's own CMD is the Lambda handler entrypoint, which expects
    # the Lambda Runtime API and just hangs locally. Override it to run
    # the polling loop instead.
    entrypoint: ["python", "notifier.py"]
    restart: unless-stopped
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "sh", "-c", "tr '\\0' ' ' < /proc/1/cmdline | grep -q notifier.py"]
      interval: 10s
      timeout: 3s
      retries: 3
      start_period: 5s

volumes:
  pgdata:

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs both test suites in containers against the compose db. Fixtures
# use the owner (admin) role; the code under test connects as its real
# least-privilege app role, so migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql is
# actually exercised, not just assumed correct.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.."

ADMIN_URL="postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis"
PORTAL_URL="postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
NOTIFIER_URL="postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
# Fixed test-only token, not a secret — raw value "test-token".
TEST_TOKEN="test-token"
TEST_TOKEN_HASH="[REDACTED:TEST_TOKEN_SHA256]"

echo "==> building images"
docker compose build db migrate portal notifier >/dev/null

echo "==> db + migrate"
docker compose up -d --wait db migrate

echo "==> portal tests (as portal_app)"
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$PORTAL_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -e API_TOKENS="tester:${TEST_TOKEN_HASH}" \
  -e TEST_TOKEN="$TEST_TOKEN" \
  --entrypoint node \
  portal --test src/app.test.js

echo "==> notifier tests (as notifier_app)"
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$NOTIFIER_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  notifier -c "pip install --quiet -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -v"

echo "==> all tests passed"

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs both test suites in containers against the compose db. Fixtures
# use the owner (admin) role; the code under test connects as its real
# least-privilege app role, so migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql is
# actually exercised, not just assumed correct.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.."

ADMIN_URL="postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis"
PORTAL_URL="postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
NOTIFIER_URL="postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
# Fixed test-only token, not a secret — raw value "test-token".
TEST_TOKEN="test-token"
TEST_TOKEN_HASH="[REDACTED:TEST_TOKEN_SHA256]"

echo "==> building images"
docker compose build db migrate portal notifier >/dev/null

echo "==> db + migrate"
docker compose up -d --wait db migrate

echo "==> portal tests (as portal_app)"
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$PORTAL_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -e API_TOKENS="tester:${TEST_TOKEN_HASH}" \
  -e TEST_TOKEN="$TEST_TOKEN" \
  --entrypoint node \
  portal --test src/app.test.js

echo "==> notifier tests (as notifier_app)"
# The image only COPYs notifier.py (see notifier/Dockerfile — it's the
# real Lambda build, kept minimal on purpose); mount the test file and
# dev requirements in on top rather than adding them to the image.
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$NOTIFIER_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/test_notifier.py:/var/task/test_notifier.py:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements.txt:/var/task/requirements.txt:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements-dev.txt:/var/task/requirements-dev.txt:ro" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  notifier -c "pip install --quiet -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -v"

echo "==> all tests passed"

# wellis-status

Internal tool for the Wellis care team: look patients up, queue appointment
reminders.

**If you're here for the take-home, start with [ASSIGNMENT.md](ASSIGNMENT.md).**
Then read [RUNBOOK.md](RUNBOOK.md), the handover memo from the people who have
been running this system.

All data in this repository is synthetic. No real person appears in it.

## Run it locally

```
docker compose up -d db
psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/wellis" < migrations/001_init.sql
psql "postgresql://postgres:postgres@127.0.0.1:5432/wellis" < migrations/002_add_index.sql
python3 scripts/seed_db.py
docker compose up -d --build portal notifier
curl http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/summary
```

## Layout

- `portal/` — Node/Express API (port 8080)
- `notifier/` — Python reminder sender
- `migrations/` — SQL, applied by hand in order
- `infra/` — how the environment was built (no IaC yet)

## Run it locally

```
make up
```

One command, no `.env` file needed. Builds the images, brings up Postgres,
runs migrations as the owner, seeds demo data, then starts `portal` and
`notifier` connected as their own least-privilege roles. Prints the URL and
a couple of `curl` examples (portal requires `Authorization: Bearer
<token>` on everything under `/api` — a fixed, local-only dev token is
printed with it).

`make down` tears the stack down, `make logs` tails it, `make test` runs
both test suites in containers against the compose DB — as the app roles,
not the owner, so the grants in `migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql` are
actually exercised.

Note: `migrations/003_rename_name_column.sql` is a known-breaking
migration, deliberately left as-is and not yet applied — see
`FINDINGS.md` (DATA-01/DATA-02). `make up` will fail at the `migrate` step
until that's resolved in a later change.

- `portal/` — Node/Express API (port 8080)
- `notifier/` — Python reminder sender; same image runs as a Lambda
  handler or, locally, as a polling loop
- `migrations/` — SQL, applied in order by `scripts/migrate.sh`
- `db/init/` — local-only: creates the app DB roles (Terraform does this
  in prod)
- `infra/` — how the environment was built (no IaC yet)
- `scripts/` — deploy, migrate, seed, test
- `ops/` — crontab, team/access notes
- `Makefile` — `up` / `down` / `test` / `logs`

Done. Nothing committed. `git status --short` shows exactly the files below, nothing else touched (verified diff is empty on infra/, scripts/deploy.sh, ops/, migrations/001-003). migrations/003 was moved aside, `make up` verified, then moved back — MD5 confirmed byte-identical to before (6dfa242cccca436bfee33eec1543e30b).

## Review fixes, done first as asked

1. Pins bumped to real, current PyPI versions (checked live, not guessed): `psycopg2-binary==2.9.13`, `boto3==1.43.101`, `pytest==9.1.1` (9.x exists for real). Built and ran the full notifier image on `public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.13` — psycopg2-binary 2.9.13 has a cp313 wheel, installs and imports cleanly, all 6 notifier tests passed on Python 3.13.15.
2. `portal/src/db.js`: added `pool.on('error', ...)` (logs, doesn't crash) and `max: Number(process.env.PG_POOL_MAX || 5)`.

## Commit groups

**1. Portal DB resilience + dependency pins** — `portal/src/db.js`, `notifier/requirements.txt`, `notifier/requirements-dev.txt`

**2. Dockerfiles** — `portal/Dockerfile` (node:24-alpine, `npm ci --omit=dev`, `USER node`, Lambda Web Adapter copied in, `AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PATH=/healthz`), `notifier/Dockerfile` (`public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.13`, AWS's own build pattern, `CMD ["notifier.handler"]`)

**3. DB roles + grants** — `db/init/01_roles.sql` (new, local-only role creation), `migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql` (new, column grants)

**4. Migration runner** — `scripts/migrate.sh` (new)

**5. Compose + Makefile + one-command bring-up** — `docker-compose.yml`, `Makefile` (new), `scripts/test.sh` (new), `scripts/seed_db.py`, `portal/src/app.test.js`, `notifier/test_notifier.py`, `README.md`

(5 groups, not 3-4 — this task had more independent moving parts than task 2. Groups 3+4 could be squashed into one if you'd rather.)

## `make up` (trimmed, 003 moved aside for this run)

```
 Container wellis-devops-db-1        Healthy
 Container wellis-devops-migrate-1   Exited (0)
 Container wellis-devops-seed-1      Exited (0)
 Container wellis-devops-notifier-1  Healthy
 Container wellis-devops-portal-1    Healthy

portal:  http://127.0.0.1:8080
  curl -s http://127.0.0.1:8080/healthz
  curl -s -H 'Authorization: Bearer [REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN]' http://127.0.0.1:8080/api/summary
```
Verified live: `/healthz` → `{"ok":true}` 200. `/api/summary` with token → `{"patients":2600,"queued_reminders":40}` 200. Same without token → `{"error":"unauthorized"}` 401. Seeded a due reminder by hand and watched the notifier pick it up within 30s: `{"event":"send_dry_run",...}` → `{"event":"sent",...}` → DB row flipped to `sent`. Confirmed via `\dp`/`information_schema.column_privileges` that portal_app/notifier_app have exactly the grants in migration 004, and confirmed negatively too — `psql -U portal_app -c "INSERT INTO patients..."` → `permission denied`, `psql -U notifier_app -c "SELECT full_name..."` → `permission denied`.

**With 003 restored** (the real, delivered state): `make up` fails cleanly at `migrate`, exit 3 — as expected and as you described. Logs show 003 itself actually applied without error this run (table was empty at that point, so `UPDATE 0` — no rows to break), but **004 then fails**: `column "full_name" of relation "patients" does not exist`, because 003 renamed it. Flagging this clearly since it's new information: migration 004 is correct against today's live schema, but once 003 is eventually resolved, 004 will need a matching update (either back to `full_name` or forward to `last_name`/`first_name`, depending how that later task resolves 003). Not something I fixed myself — didn't know how you're planning to resolve 003, and you said not to edit it.

## `make test` (trimmed)

```
==> portal tests (as portal_app)
✔ GET /healthz needs no auth
✔ GET /api/patients without a token is 401
✔ GET /api/patients with a wrong token is 401
✔ SQL injection payload returns an empty array, not an error or every row
✔ normal lookup returns the matching patient
✔ POST /api/reminders rejects invalid input with 400
✔ POST /api/reminders queues a valid reminder
ℹ tests 7, pass 7, fail 0

==> notifier tests (as notifier_app)
test_notifier.py::test_send_one_true_when_http_call_succeeds PASSED
test_notifier.py::test_send_one_false_when_http_call_raises PASSED
test_notifier.py::test_send_one_true_in_dry_run_with_no_messaging_url PASSED
test_notifier.py::test_fetch_due_only_returns_due_reminders PASSED
test_notifier.py::test_failed_send_leaves_reminder_queued PASSED
test_notifier.py::test_successful_send_marks_reminder_sent PASSED
6 passed in 0.53s
==> all tests passed
```
Both suites genuinely run as the app roles (`portal_app`/`notifier_app`), not the owner — fixtures go through a separate `ADMIN_DATABASE_URL` connection. Ran on Python 3.13.15 / pytest 9.1.1 inside the actual notifier image.

## Things I had to decide myself

- **`AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PATH`** as the Lambda Web Adapter's readiness-path env var — from training knowledge, not verified against live docs. Everything I *could* verify locally (adapter binary present at `/opt/extensions/lambda-adapter`, correct size/perms, container runs fine as non-root) checks out, but the adapter is inert locally by design, so this specific env var name is worth a quick sanity check against AWS's docs before a real Lambda deploy.
- **Postgres 18's changed volume convention**: the image now wants the volume mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql`, not `.../data` — `db` failed to start with the obvious mount, fixed and commented in compose. Pure discovery from testing, not something flagged going in.
- **`seed` reuses the notifier image** (`build: ./notifier`, entrypoint override) rather than a third Dockerfile, since it already has psycopg2. Had to add `PYTHONPATH=/var/task` for it — the Lambda base image only puts pip's `--target /var/task` packages on `sys.path` by accident for `notifier.py` itself (because that script's own directory *is* `/var/task`); a script mounted elsewhere (`/scripts/seed_db.py`) can't see them without it.
- **`docker compose up --wait` doesn't handle a directly-targeted one-shot service** — it reports failure even on exit 0. `make up`'s own flow avoids this because portal/seed reference `migrate` via `depends_on: condition: service_completed_successfully`, which works fine; `scripts/test.sh` had to be restructured to `up --wait db` then a separate `run --rm migrate` instead of `up --wait db migrate`.
- **Notifier healthcheck** uses `grep notifier.py /proc/1/cmdline` (via `tr`+`grep`) rather than adding a heartbeat file to `notifier.py` — it's not an HTTP service, and a heartbeat mechanism felt like scope beyond "add healthchecks."
- **Fixed dev/test tokens are hardcoded** (`[REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN]` for compose, `test-token` for `scripts/test.sh`) including their precomputed sha256 hashes, rather than computed at script-run-time via `shasum`/`sha256sum` — avoids a portability dependency across dev machines. Both are clearly commented as local-only, not secrets.
- **No automated test for the new `pool.on('error')` handler** — reliably forcing Postgres to drop an idle connection mid-test felt like more machinery than it's worth here. Verified by code review only; flagging as a real coverage gap rather than silently skipping it.
- **`db/init/01_roles.sql` has no idempotency guard** on `CREATE ROLE` — relies on `docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` only running once on first init, which is standard Postgres image behavior, not something that needed defending against.

## Commit groups

**1. Portal DB resilience + dependency pins** — `portal/src/db.js`, `notifier/requirements.txt`, `notifier/requirements-dev.txt`

Verified live: `/healthz` → `{"ok":true}` 200. `/api/summary` with token → `{"patients":2600,"queued_reminders":40}` 200. Same without token → `{"error":"unauthorized"}` 401. Seeded a due reminder by hand and watched the notifier pick it up within 30s: `{"event":"send_dry_run",...}` → `{"event":"sent",...}` → DB row flipped to `sent`. **With 003 restored** (the real, delivered state): `make up` fails cleanly at `migrate`, exit 3 — as expected and as you described. Flagging this clearly since it's new information: migration 004 is correct against today's live schema, but once 003 is eventually resolved, 004 will need a matching update (either back to `full_name` or forward to `last_name`/`first_name`, depending how that later task resolves 003). Both suites genuinely run as the app roles (`portal_app`/`notifier_app`), not the owner — fixtures go through a separate `ADMIN_DATABASE_URL` connection. Ran on Python 3.13.15 / pytest 9.1.1 inside the actual notifier image.

## Things I had to decide myself

- **`AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PATH`** as the Lambda Web Adapter's readiness-path env var — from training knowledge, not verified against live docs. Everything I *could* verify locally (adapter binary present at `/opt/extensions/lambda-adapter`, correct size/perms, container runs fine as non-root) checks out, but the adapter is inert locally by design, so this specific env var name is worth a quick sanity check against AWS's docs before a real Lambda deploy.
- **Postgres 18's changed volume convention**: the image now wants the volume mounted at `/var/lib/postgresql`, not `.../data` — `db` failed to start with the obvious mount, fixed and commented in compose. Pure discovery from testing, not something flagged going in.
- **`seed` reuses the notifier image** (`build: ./notifier`, entrypoint override) rather than a third Dockerfile, since it already has psycopg2. Had to add `PYTHONPATH=/var/task` for it — the Lambda base image only puts pip's `--target /var/task` packages on `sys.path` by accident for `notifier.py` itself (because that script's own directory *is* `/var/task`); a script mounted elsewhere (`/scripts/seed_db.py`) can't see them without it.
- **`docker compose up --wait` doesn't handle a directly-targeted one-shot service** — it reports failure even on exit 0. `make up`'s own flow avoids this because portal/seed reference `migrate` via `depends_on: condition: service_completed_successfully`, which works fine; `scripts/test.sh` had to be restructured to `up --wait db` then a separate `run --rm migrate` instead of `up --wait db migrate`.
- **Notifier healthcheck** uses `grep notifier.py /proc/1/cmdline` (via `tr`+`grep`) rather than adding a heartbeat file to `notifier.py` — it's not an HTTP service, and a heartbeat mechanism felt like scope beyond "add healthchecks."
- **Fixed dev/test tokens are hardcoded** (`[REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN]` for compose, `test-token` for `scripts/test.sh`) including their precomputed sha256 hashes, rather than computed at script-run-time via `shasum`/`sha256sum` — avoids a portability dependency across dev machines. Both are clearly commented as local-only, not secrets.
- **No automated test for the new `pool.on('error')` handler** — reliably forcing Postgres to drop an idle connection mid-test felt like more machinery than it's worth here. Verified by code review only; flagging as a real coverage gap rather than silently skipping it.
- **`db/init/01_roles.sql` has no idempotency guard** on `CREATE ROLE` — relies on `docker-entrypoint-initdb.d` only running once on first init, which is standard Postgres image behavior, not something that needed defending against.

# squawk config for wellis-status migrations.
#
# Default-on: every rule squawk ships stays enabled unless it's listed
# below, with a reason. This is a short denylist, not a curated allowlist
# — the rules the brief called out by name (renames, adding NOT NULL,
# non-concurrent index) are not listed here because they need to stay on.
#
# Scope: only migrations/003 onward get linted at all — see
# .github/workflows/ci.yml, which excludes 001/002 from the squawk
# invocation. 001/002 were already applied to the real prod DB by hand
# before this pipeline existed (see RUNBOOK.md); linting settled history
# that can't be changed is noise, not signal.

pg_version = "18.0"

excluded_rules = [
  # scripts/migrate.sh sets lock_timeout and statement_timeout for every
  # migration it runs, via PGOPTIONS, before psql ever opens the file —
  # see the runner's own header comment. Requiring a matching `SET`
  # statement inside each .sql file on top of that would be redundant,
  # not an extra safety net.
  "require-lock-timeout",
  "require-statement-timeout",

  # scripts/migrate.sh already wraps each file in its own BEGIN/COMMIT
  # and records it in schema_migrations before moving to the next one, so
  # a file is never re-run after a partial failure. That's what this rule
  # checks for (IF NOT EXISTS, explicit transactions) — handled one level
  # up, by the runner, not per-statement in the SQL itself.
  "prefer-robust-stmts",

  # Schema-design taste (serial/int vs identity/bigint), not a live-table
  # locking/breakage risk, and not worth relitigating on every migration
  # for id columns that already exist in prod.
  "prefer-bigint-over-int",
  "prefer-identity",
]

| ID | Title | Where | Why it matters | Severity | Status |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| SEC-04 | Live secrets committed to git, never rotated | `.env:6-8`, `.env.staging:6-8`; introduced commit `90c1d36`, `7ddfec0` | Real-shaped DB password + a `live_`-prefixed messaging API key sit in plaintext in the repo history; staging reuses the exact same DB password and key as prod — one leak compromises both | critical | TBD |
| SEC-05 | GCP service-account key was committed to git history | `sa-key.json` added in `03873fd`, untracked (not deleted from history) in `15a128a` | The key is already present in every existing clone; deleting the file from the tip and adding it to `.gitignore` doesn't revoke exposure. **Rotating the key is the actual fix.** A history rewrite is optional and, on its own, un-leaks nothing for anyone who already has a clone | critical | TBD |
| SEC-06 | The leaked service-account key is `roles/owner` on the whole GCP project | `infra/PROVISIONING.md` (`ops-sa@...`, `roles/owner`) | It's provisioned only to write to one GCS bucket. A leaked key (see SEC-05) hands over the entire project — compute, IAM, billing, everything — not just the receipts bucket | critical | TBD |
| SEC-07 | App and notifier both connect to Postgres as the `postgres` superuser | `portal/src/db.js:3-9`; `notifier/notifier.py` DB dict | No least privilege at the DB layer; the SQL injection in SEC-01 (or any future bug) has full superuser reach, not just `patients`/`reminders` | high | TBD |
| SEC-10 | Staging runs on the live/production messaging key | `.env.staging:8` (`MESSAGING_KEY=[REDACTED:MESSAGING_KEY]`, same value as `.env:8`) | This is separate from "the secrets are reused" (SEC-04): because the key is live, anything sent from staging is a **real message through the real provider account** to whatever address is in the staging DB — testing against staging can actually page/text real people | critical | TBD |
| SEC-15 | `RECEIPT_BUCKET` defaults to the prod bucket name in code | `notifier/notifier.py:26` (`RECEIPT_BUCKET = os.environ.get("RECEIPT_BUCKET", "wellis-receipts-prod")`) | Any environment where this var is missing or misconfigured — a future local run, a new environment, a typo'd env file — silently writes real receipt data (PHI, see APP-10) into the **production** bucket instead of failing loudly or writing nowhere | high | TBD |

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs both test suites in containers against the compose db. Fixtures
# use the owner (admin) role; the code under test connects as its real
# least-privilege app role, so migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql is
# actually exercised, not just assumed correct.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.."

ADMIN_URL="postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis"
PORTAL_URL="postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
NOTIFIER_URL="postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
# Fixed test-only token, not a secret — raw value "test-token".
TEST_TOKEN="test-token"
TEST_TOKEN_HASH="[REDACTED:TEST_TOKEN_SHA256]"

echo "==> building images"
docker compose build db migrate portal notifier >/dev/null

echo "==> db"
docker compose up -d --wait db

echo "==> migrate"
# `up --wait` doesn't handle a one-shot service well (it flags any exit,
# even 0, as failure) — `run` blocks and gives us the real exit code.
docker compose run --rm migrate

echo "==> portal tests (as portal_app)"
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$PORTAL_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -e API_TOKENS="tester:${TEST_TOKEN_HASH}" \
  -e TEST_TOKEN="$TEST_TOKEN" \
  --entrypoint node \
  portal --test src/app.test.js

echo "==> notifier tests (as notifier_app)"
# The image only COPYs notifier.py (see notifier/Dockerfile — it's the
# real Lambda build, kept minimal on purpose); mount the test file and
# dev requirements in on top rather than adding them to the image.
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$NOTIFIER_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/test_notifier.py:/var/task/test_notifier.py:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements.txt:/var/task/requirements.txt:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements-dev.txt:/var/task/requirements-dev.txt:ro" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  notifier -c "pip install --quiet -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -v"

echo "==> all tests passed"

PORTAL_URL="postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
NOTIFIER_URL="postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
# Fixed test-only token, not a secret — raw value "test-token".
TEST_TOKEN="test-token"
TEST_TOKEN_HASH="[REDACTED:TEST_TOKEN_SHA256]"

echo "==> building images"
docker compose build db migrate portal notifier >/dev/null

echo "==> db"
docker compose up -d --wait db

echo "==> migrate"
# `up --wait` doesn't handle a one-shot service well (it flags any exit,
# even 0, as failure) — `run` blocks and gives us the real exit code.
docker compose run --rm migrate

echo "==> portal tests (as portal_app)"
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$PORTAL_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -e API_TOKENS="tester:${TEST_TOKEN_HASH}" \
  -e TEST_TOKEN="$TEST_TOKEN" \
  --entrypoint node \
  portal --test src/app.test.js

echo "==> notifier tests (as notifier_app)"
# The image only COPYs notifier.py (see notifier/Dockerfile — it's the
# real Lambda build, kept minimal on purpose); mount the test file and
# dev requirements in on top rather than adding them to the image.
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$NOTIFIER_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/test_notifier.py:/var/task/test_notifier.py:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements.txt:/var/task/requirements.txt:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements-dev.txt:/var/task/requirements-dev.txt:ro" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  notifier -c "pip install --quiet -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -v"

echo "==> all tests passed"

# Same image locally and on Lambda. The Lambda Web Adapter is a Lambda
# extension: outside Lambda (docker run / compose) nothing invokes it, so
# it's inert and the container just runs the normal HTTP server.
FROM node:24-alpine

WORKDIR /app

COPY package.json package-lock.json ./
RUN npm ci --omit=dev

COPY --from=public.ecr.aws/awsguru/aws-lambda-adapter:1.1.0 /lambda-adapter /opt/extensions/lambda-adapter

COPY . .

USER node

ENV PORT=8080 \
    AWS_LWA_READINESS_CHECK_PATH=/healthz

EXPOSE 8080
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]

name: CI

on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]

concurrency:
  group: ${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true

permissions:
  contents: read

jobs:
  # Same path a developer uses: `make up` then `make test`. This is also
  # the only thing that actually proves the one-command bring-up works,
  # not just that the individual pieces build.
  #
  # Expected to be red right now: migrations/003_rename_name_column.sql
  # renames a column both migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql and the
  # already-committed app code depend on by the old name, so `make up`
  # fails at the migrate step. See FINDINGS.md DATA-01/DATA-02 — this is
  # known, on purpose, and gets fixed in the next change, not here.
  test:
    name: test
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - name: checkout
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: bring up the stack and run tests
        run: |
          make up
          make test

      - name: dump compose logs
        if: failure()
        run: docker compose logs

      - name: tear down
        if: always()

input.message:
Done. Nothing committed. `git status --short`:
```
 M Makefile              (inline gitleaks:allow on the [REDACTED:DEV_TOKEN] curl example)
 M portal/Dockerfile     (strip npm after install — see trivy section)
 M scripts/test.sh       (inline gitleaks:allow on the test-token hash)
?? .github/workflows/ci.yml
?? .gitleaksignore
?? .squawk.toml
?? .trivyignore
```

## The workflow — `.github/workflows/ci.yml`

`on: pull_request` + `push: branches: [main]`. Concurrency group `${{ github.workflow }}-${{ github.ref }}` with `cancel-in-progress: true`. Top-level `permissions: contents: read`, nothing needs more. Four independent jobs (no `needs:`, they run in parallel), all pinned: `actions/checkout@v4`, `ghcr.io/sbdchd/squawk:2.66.0`, `zricethezav/gitleaks:v8.30.1`, `aquasec/trivy:0.74.0` — all real, current released versions, not `latest`. Every tool runs via plain `docker run`, the same invocations I tested locally below, so `docker run ...` from the workflow is copy-pasteable and reproduces CI exactly — no marketplace-action indirection to second-guess.

## Local results, in CI order

**1. `test`** (`make up` && `make test`, dump `docker compose logs` on failure, always tear down) — **red, expected**. `make up` fails at the `migrate` step (exit 3) with 003 in place. Confirmed via the compose-logs dump this is the exact issue I flagged after task 3: migration 004's `GRANT SELECT (id, full_name, ...)` fails because 003 already renamed `full_name` → `last_name`:
```
db-1 | ERROR:  column "full_name" of relation "patients" does not exist
db-1 | STATEMENT:  GRANT SELECT (id, full_name, email, dob) ON patients TO portal_app;
```
So this job is red for the same underlying reason as `migration-lint`, not a separate problem — worth knowing going in, since "everything else should be green" doesn't quite hold: two jobs go red on the first push, both tracing back to 003.

**2. `migration-lint`** — **red, expected**. Lints `migrations/003` onward (001/002 excluded by filename, computed dynamically via `find ... ! -name '001_*' ! -name '002_*'`, so a future 005 gets linted automatically without editing the workflow again). Output:
```
migrations/003_rename_name_column.sql:6:21: warning: renaming-column ...
migrations/003_rename_name_column.sql:9:45: warning: adding-not-nullable-field ...
exit 1
```
004 is clean. `.squawk.toml` excludes 4 rules, each with a reason: `require-lock-timeout`/`require-statement-timeout` (scripts/migrate.sh already sets both via PGOPTIONS for every migration it runs — redundant to also demand it per-file), `prefer-robust-stmts` (migrate.sh already wraps each file in its own transaction and tracks it in schema_migrations — the exact thing this rule checks for), `prefer-bigint-over-int`/`prefer-identity` (schema-design taste, not live-table risk, for columns that already exist in prod). `renaming-column`, `adding-not-nullable-field`, `require-concurrent-index-creation` are untouched and stay on.

**3. `secrets`** — will be **green once committed**, currently shows 2 findings locally and I want to be precise about why rather than just assert it's fine. `gitleaks detect` scans git *history*, not the working tree, and I was told not to commit — so the two inline `# gitleaks:allow` comments I just added to `Makefile` and `scripts/test.sh` aren't in any commit yet, and the historical (uncommitted) version of those lines still matches. I verified the mechanism two ways instead of just trusting it: (a) `--no-git` mode, which scans the working tree as plain files, confirms both inline-allow comments correctly suppress their matches; (b) the normal history scan already shows the 6 real old/cited secrets correctly suppressed via `.gitleaksignore` fingerprints, since those were already committed. `.gitleaksignore` covers: `.env`'s and `.env.staging`'s `DB_PASSWORD`/`MESSAGING_KEY` (4 fingerprints), `sa-key.json`'s private key, and one more I hadn't anticipated — FINDINGS.md quotes that same `MESSAGING_KEY` value verbatim while documenting SEC-04/SEC-10, so gitleaks flags it too; same burned secret, not a new one, so it's in the ignore file with a comment rather than edited (FINDINGS.md isn't mine to touch here). Once this is committed, `gitleaks detect --source . --no-banner` should exit 0 — I can't fully prove that locally by design, but every individual piece is verified.

**4. `images`** — **green**, and this one needed a real fix, not just documentation. Built both images fresh and ran `trivy image --severity CRITICAL,HIGH --ignore-unfixed`:
- **portal**: 4 HIGH findings, all inside npm's own bundled internal deps (`brace-expansion`, `ip-address`, `tar`, under `node_modules/npm/node_modules/...`) — not our dependencies, and npm is never invoked at runtime (`CMD` is `node`, not `npm start`). Since this is something we control (we chose to keep npm around after `npm ci`), I fixed it rather than excluded it: `portal/Dockerfile` now does `rm -rf /usr/local/lib/node_modules/npm /usr/local/bin/npm /usr/local/bin/npx` right after `npm ci --omit=dev` finishes. Rebuilt, confirmed the container still runs correctly as the `node` user, rescanned: 0 findings, exit 0.
- **notifier**: 2 HIGH findings — `msgpack` (GHSA-6v7p-g79w-8964) and `setuptools` (CVE-2025-47273). Traced both by hand before deciding what to do: `msgpack` is pip's own vendored copy at `.../site-packages/pip/_vendor/msgpack` (confirmed `import msgpack` fails in the running container — it's not a real top-level package); `setuptools` is a static `.whl` file sitting in CPython's own standard-library test fixtures (`.../test/wheeldata/setuptools-79.0.1-py3-none-any.whl`), never installed or imported. Both are baked into `public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.13` itself — AWS's official base image, which was an explicit choice in task 3, not something I should start deleting stdlib test data or pip internals out of. These went in `.trivyignore` with the file paths and how I confirmed them, not just the CVE IDs blind. Rescanned with `.trivyignore` applied: 0 findings, exit 0. Every one of our actual dependencies (boto3, botocore, psycopg2-binary, etc.) shows clean.

## Anything noisy I had to exclude

Covered above inline, but to summarize the judgment calls: 4 squawk rules (reasoned, in `.squawk.toml`), 6 gitleaks fingerprints for old secrets + 1 for FINDINGS.md's citation of one of them (in `.gitleaksignore`), 2 inline gitleaks allows for my own local-only dev/test tokens (not secrets, just pattern-matched), and 2 trivy CVEs that are inert base-image-internal artifacts (in `.trivyignore`, with the exact file paths I found them at). Nothing in `.trivyignore` or `.gitleaksignore` covers anything in our own code or dependencies — every exclusion is either settled history, or something bundled by a base image we didn't choose the internals of.

# wellis-status

Internal tool for the Wellis care team: look patients up, queue appointment
reminders.

**If you're here for the take-home, start with [ASSIGNMENT.md](ASSIGNMENT.md).**
Then read [RUNBOOK.md](RUNBOOK.md), the handover memo from the people who have
been running this system.

All data in this repository is synthetic. No real person appears in it.

## Run it locally

```
make up
```

One command, no `.env` file needed. Builds the images, brings up Postgres,
runs migrations as the owner, seeds demo data, then starts `portal` and
`notifier` connected as their own least-privilege roles. Prints the URL and
a couple of `curl` examples (portal requires `Authorization: Bearer
<token>` on everything under `/api` — a fixed, local-only dev token is
printed with it).

`make down` tears the stack down, `make logs` tails it, `make test` runs
both test suites in containers against the compose DB — as the app roles,
not the owner, so the grants in `migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql` are
actually exercised.

Note: `migrations/003_rename_name_column.sql` is a known-breaking
migration, deliberately left as-is and not yet applied — see
`FINDINGS.md` (DATA-01/DATA-02). `make up` will fail at the `migrate` step
until that's resolved in a later change.

## Layout

- `portal/` — Node/Express API (port 8080)
- `notifier/` — Python reminder sender; same image runs as a Lambda
  handler or, locally, as a polling loop
- `migrations/` — SQL, applied in order by `scripts/migrate.sh`
- `db/init/` — local-only: creates the app DB roles (Terraform does this
  in prod)
- `infra/` — how the environment was built (no IaC yet)
- `scripts/` — deploy, migrate, seed, test
- `ops/` — crontab, team/access notes
- `Makefile` — `up` / `down` / `test` / `logs`

-- Product wants first/last split instead of one name field. Replaces the
-- original 003 (see git history / FINDINGS.md DATA-01/DATA-02/DATA-03),
-- which renamed full_name in place and broke every reader of it, wasn't
-- transactional, and mis-split the data. Never applied anywhere — 001
-- and 002 are the only migrations that have run against real data, so
-- there was nothing to migrate away from.
--
-- This version is expand-only: full_name stays, unchanged, as the
-- source of truth. Nothing here can break an existing reader. 004 and
-- the app code keep using full_name — that doesn't change in this
-- migration.
--
-- Contract plan (future migrations, not this one):
--   005: app code switches to reading first_name/last_name instead of
--        full_name, deployed and verified first.
--   006: ADD CONSTRAINT ... CHECK (first_name IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID,
--        then VALIDATE CONSTRAINT in a separate statement/transaction —
--        not a plain SET NOT NULL, which takes ACCESS EXCLUSIVE for a
--        full-table scan (see squawk's adding-not-nullable-field, and
--        the old 003's own DATA-02 finding).
--   much later: drop full_name, once nothing reads it.
--
-- Backfill note: this runs the split against every existing row in one
-- UPDATE. Fine at today's ~2,600 rows; on a real-sized table this would
-- need to be batched (e.g. by id range) and run outside this migration,
-- because scripts/migrate.sh sets a 60s statement_timeout on purpose —
-- it's there to fail fast instead of queueing behind the notifier, not
-- a budget to design a backfill around.

ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN first_name TEXT;
ALTER TABLE patients ADD COLUMN last_name TEXT;

-- Nothing in the app writes patients (only scripts/seed_db.py does, and
-- it runs after this migration, as the owner) — but without this,
-- every row inserted from here on would have first_name/last_name stuck
-- NULL until someone remembered to backfill it again. Keeps the split in
-- sync with full_name for any future insert/update, not just today's.
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION patients_set_first_last_name() RETURNS trigger AS $$
BEGIN
    NEW.first_name := split_part(NEW.full_name, ' ', 1);
    IF position(' ' IN NEW.full_name) = 0 THEN
        NEW.last_name := NULL;
    ELSE
        NEW.last_name := substring(NEW.full_name FROM position(' ' IN NEW.full_name) + 1);
    END IF;
    RETURN NEW;
END;
$$ LANGUAGE plpgsql;

CREATE TRIGGER patients_first_last_name_trigger
    BEFORE INSERT OR UPDATE OF full_name ON patients
    FOR EACH ROW
    EXECUTE FUNCTION patients_set_first_last_name();

-- Backfill: first word -> first_name, the rest -> last_name.
-- "Sanne de Vries" -> first_name "Sanne", last_name "de Vries".
-- "Bram" (no space) -> first_name "Bram", last_name NULL.
-- WHERE guard makes this idempotent/resumable, not just a one-shot.
UPDATE patients
SET first_name = split_part(full_name, ' ', 1),
    last_name = CASE
        WHEN position(' ' IN full_name) = 0 THEN NULL
        ELSE substring(full_name FROM position(' ' IN full_name) + 1)
    END
WHERE first_name IS NULL;

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Runs both test suites in containers against the compose db. Fixtures
# use the owner (admin) role; the code under test connects as its real
# least-privilege app role, so migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql is
# actually exercised, not just assumed correct.
set -euo pipefail
cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")/.."

ADMIN_URL="postgresql://postgres:postgres@db:5432/wellis"
PORTAL_URL="postgresql://portal_app:portal_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
NOTIFIER_URL="postgresql://notifier_app:notifier_app_dev_password@db:5432/wellis"
# Fixed test-only token, not a secret — raw value "test-token".
TEST_TOKEN="test-token"
TEST_TOKEN_HASH="[REDACTED:TEST_TOKEN_SHA256]" # gitleaks:allow — sha256 of "test-token" above, not a secret

echo "==> building images"
docker compose build db migrate portal notifier >/dev/null

echo "==> db"
docker compose up -d --wait db

echo "==> migrate"
# `up --wait` doesn't handle a one-shot service well (it flags any exit,
# even 0, as failure) — `run` blocks and gives us the real exit code.
docker compose run --rm migrate

echo "==> portal tests (as portal_app)"
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$PORTAL_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -e API_TOKENS="tester:${TEST_TOKEN_HASH}" \
  -e TEST_TOKEN="$TEST_TOKEN" \
  --entrypoint node \
  portal --test src/app.test.js

echo "==> notifier tests (as notifier_app)"
# The image only COPYs notifier.py (see notifier/Dockerfile — it's the
# real Lambda build, kept minimal on purpose); mount the test file and
# dev requirements in on top rather than adding them to the image.
docker compose run --rm --no-deps \
  -e DATABASE_URL="$NOTIFIER_URL" \
  -e ADMIN_DATABASE_URL="$ADMIN_URL" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/test_notifier.py:/var/task/test_notifier.py:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements.txt:/var/task/requirements.txt:ro" \
  -v "$(pwd)/notifier/requirements-dev.txt:/var/task/requirements-dev.txt:ro" \
  --entrypoint sh \
  notifier -c "pip install --quiet -r requirements-dev.txt && pytest -v"

echo "==> all tests passed"

# wellis-status

Internal tool for the Wellis care team: look patients up, queue appointment
reminders.

**If you're here for the take-home, start with [ASSIGNMENT.md](ASSIGNMENT.md).**
Then read [RUNBOOK.md](RUNBOOK.md), the handover memo from the people who have
been running this system.

All data in this repository is synthetic. No real person appears in it.

## Run it locally

```
make up
```

One command, no `.env` file needed. Builds the images, brings up Postgres,
runs migrations as the owner, seeds demo data, then starts `portal` and
`notifier` connected as their own least-privilege roles. Prints the URL and
a couple of `curl` examples (portal requires `Authorization: Bearer
<token>` on everything under `/api` — a fixed, local-only dev token is
printed with it).

`make down` tears the stack down, `make logs` tails it, `make test` runs
both test suites in containers against the compose DB — as the app roles,
not the owner, so the grants in `migrations/004_app_role_grants.sql` are
actually exercised.

Note: `migrations/003_rename_name_column.sql` is a known-breaking
migration, deliberately left as-is and not yet applied — see
`FINDINGS.md` (DATA-01/DATA-02). `make up` will fail at the `migrate` step
until that's resolved in a later change.

## Layout

- `portal/` — Node/Express API (port 8080)
- `notifier/` — Python reminder sender; same image runs as a Lambda
  handler or, locally, as a polling loop
- `migrations/` — SQL, applied in order by `scripts/migrate.sh`
- `db/init/` — local-only: creates the app DB roles (Terraform does this
  in prod)
- `infra/` — how the environment was built (no IaC yet)
- `scripts/` — deploy, migrate, seed, test
- `ops/` — crontab, team/access notes
- `Makefile` — `up` / `down` / `test` / `logs`

The coordinator sent a message while you were working:
Task 6: Terraform for AWS + Neon. Write and plan it only; I do the applies. Your 003 is committed and CI is re-running. The first run went red on the old 003, exactly as planned.

Target: AWS eu-central-1 (the Neon project is aws-eu-central-1). Use AWS_PROFILE=backendlab-production. For Neon, `export NEON_API_KEY="$(cat ~/.config/wellis/neon_api_key)"` inline in the same command. Never print it, never write it anywhere in the repo.

Layout
- infra/terraform/bootstrap: S3 state bucket (versioned, encrypted, public access blocked, TLS-only policy) and the GitHub OIDC provider. Local state first; after I apply it, we move its state into the bucket.
- infra/terraform/prod: S3 backend with use_lockfile = true. Pin the providers: aws 6.x, kislerdm/neon, cyrilgdn/postgresql, random. default_tags project/env/managed_by.

Neon
- Existing project frosty-tree-52704700 (org org-little-feather-38495886). Try an import block with prevent_destroy. If the plan wants to replace or change anything big on the project, drop the import and reference it by id instead. Don't fight the provider.
- Create role wellis_owner and database wellis via the neon provider. Leave the demo db alone.
- The app roles must NOT be neon_role. Roles made through the Neon API join neon_superuser. Create portal_app and notifier_app with the postgresql provider, connected as wellis_owner: LOGIN and a random password only.

Secrets
- SSM SecureString under /wellis/prod/<service>/<NAME>: portal DATABASE_URL + API_TOKENS, and notifier DATABASE_URL. Use the pooler host + sslmode=require for the apps.
- A migrator DATABASE_URL (owner) on the direct host, not the pooler. The pooler doesn't pass PGOPTIONS, and migrate.sh needs its timeouts.
- Named tokens: reviewer and ci-smoke, from random_password. The hashes go in API_TOKENS; the raw values go under /wellis/prod/tokens/<name>.
- App change: when SSM_PARAMETER_PATH is set, both apps load their params from that path at cold start (GetParametersByPath with decryption) into env before anything else. Local runs keep plain env vars, so AWS stays one small optional module in each app.

Compute
- ECR: two repos, immutable tags, scan on push, keep the last 10 images.
- Lambdas: x86_64, image package type, ignore_changes on image_uri since CI deploys the code. Explicit log groups with 30-day retention.
- portal: 512MB, 10s timeout, reserved concurrency 5 (caps DB connections and cost), PG_POOL_MAX=2, Function URL with auth NONE; the app does the auth. Check whether a public function URL now needs both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction in the resource policy. AWS changed this recently; I'll verify with curl after apply.
- notifier: 256MB, 60s, reserved concurrency 1 (no overlapping runs, so no double sends). EventBridge Scheduler rate(15 minutes) with 0 retries, using its own role that can only invoke this function. 15 min because reminders are hours ahead, and it lets Neon scale to zero between runs on the free compute hours.
- Receipts bucket: private, SSE-S3, TLS-only, expire after 90 days.

IAM
- One role per function: logs to its own group, GetParametersByPath on its own path, and for the notifier PutObject on receipts/* only.
- GitHub deploy role: trust only realsby/devops-assignment on refs/heads/main. It can push to the two ECR repos, call UpdateFunctionCode/GetFunction on the two functions, and GetParameter on the migrator URL and the ci-smoke token. Nothing else.

Out of this task: monitoring (next task). Add a terraform fmt + validate job to ci.yml.

Chicken-and-egg: the Lambdas need an image at create. Plan it so I apply the ECR repos first with -target, push images (built --platform linux/amd64, tagged with the git sha), then apply the rest with var image_tag.

Stop after: bootstrap written + planned, prod written + validated. The prod plan needs the backend, so I'll ping you after the bootstrap apply. Don't commit. Reply with the file list, the bootstrap plan summary, and every place you guessed an attribute name, so I can check them.

Address this before completing your current task.

# neon_project (Resource)

Neon Project.

Note that this resource manages five resources:

- Project: https://neon.com/docs/reference/glossary#project
- Root branch: https://neon.com/docs/reference/glossary#root-branch
- Primary compute with the default read-write endpoint: https://neon.com/docs/reference/glossary#compute
- Default database: https://neon.com/docs/reference/glossary#database
- Default role: https://neon.com/docs/reference/glossary#postgres-role


## Example Usage

```terraform
### Default

resource "neon_project" "example" {
  name = "foo"
}

### Turn off data retention

resource "neon_project" "example" {
  name                      = "foo"
  history_retention_seconds = 0
}

### Set custom compute limits. Note that this configurations don't apply to existing compute,
# e.g., they don't affect the primary compute resources provisioned with the project by default.

resource "neon_project" "example" {
  name = "foo"

  autoscaling_limit_min_cu = 0.5
  autoscaling_limit_max_cu = 1
  suspend_timeout_seconds  = 10
}

### Set compute limits for the primary compute resources provisioned with the project.

resource "neon_project" "example" {
  name = "foo"

  primary_compute {
    autoscaling_limit_min_cu = 0.5
    autoscaling_limit_max_cu = 1
    suspend_timeout_seconds  = 10
  }
}


### Define custom default branch

resource "neon_project" "example" {
  name = "foo"

  branch {
    name          = "bar"
    database_name = "baz"
    role_name     = "qux"
  }
}

# neon_role (Resource)

Project Role. **Note** that User and Role are synonymous terms in Neon. 
See details: https://neon.tech/docs/manage/users/


## Example Usage

```terraform
resource "neon_project" "example" {
  name = "foo"
}

resource "neon_branch" "example" {
  project_id = neon_project.example.id
  name       = "bar"
}

resource "neon_role" "example" {
  project_id = neon_project.example.id
  branch_id  = neon_branch.example.id
  name       = "qux"
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Required

- `branch_id` (String) Branch ID.
- `name` (String) Role name.
- `project_id` (String) Project ID.

### Read-Only

- `id` (String) The ID of this resource.
- `password` (String, Sensitive) Database authentication password.
- `protected` (Boolean)



## Import

The Neon Role can be imported to the terraform state by the identifier which is composed of the `projectID`, `branchID`
and the Role `name`. For example, the identifier of the Role `myRole` from the branch `br-snowy-mountain-a5jkb18i`
of the project `shiny-cell-31746257` is `shiny-cell-31746257/br-snowy-mountain-a5jkb18i/myRole`.

Import using the [import block](https://developer.hashicorp.com/terraform/language/import):

For example:

```hcl
import {
  to = neon_role.example
  id = "shiny-cell-31746257/br-snowy-mountain-a5jkb18i/myRole"
}
```

Import using the command `terraform import`:

```commandline
terraform import neon_role.example "shiny-cell-31746257/br-snowy-mountain-a5jkb18i/myRole"
```

### Set the logical replication
# See: https://neon.tech/docs/guides/logical-replication-guide
resource "neon_project" "example_with_logical_replication" {
  name = "my-project-with-logical-replication"

  enable_logical_replication = "yes"
}

### Set the allow list of IP addresses
# Note that the feature is only available to the users of the Business plan:
# https://neon.tech/docs/introduction/ip-allow
resource "neon_project" "example_with_allowed_ips" {
  name = "my-project-with-allowed-list-of-ips"

  allowed_ips = ["1.2.3.4/24", "99.1.20.93"]
}

### Set the allow list of IP addresses for protected branches only
# Note that the feature is only available to the users of the Business, or Scale plans:
# https://neon.tech/docs/guides/protected-branches
resource "neon_project" "example_with_allowed_ips_protected_branch_only" {
  name = "my-project-with-allowed-list-of-ips-for-protected-branch"

  allowed_ips                         = ["1.2.3.4/24", "99.1.20.93"]
  allowed_ips_protected_branches_only = "yes"
}

### Block public connections to the project's endpoints
# Note that the feature is only available to the users of the Scale plans:
# https://neon.tech/docs/introduction/ip-allow
resource "neon_project" "example_with_blocked_public_connections" {
  name = "my-project-with-blocked-public-connections"

  block_public_connections = "yes"
}

### Create project in the organisation
resource "neon_project" "example_in_org" {
  name   = "myproject"
  org_id = "org-restless-silence-28866559"
}

### Set custom maintenance window
# Note that the feature is only available to the users of non-Free plan
# https://neon.com/docs/manage/updates
resource "neon_project" "custom_maintenance_window" {
  name = "myproject"
  maintenance_window {
    weekdays   = [6, 7]
    start_time = "07:00"
    end_time   = "08:00"
  }
}

### Block connections that use VPC
resource "neon_project" "example_with_blocked_vpc_connections" {
  name = "my-project-with-blocked-vpc-connections"

  block_vpc_connections = "yes"
}
```

<!-- schema generated by tfplugindocs -->
## Schema

### Optional

- `allowed_ips` (List of String) A list of IP addresses that are allowed to connect to the endpoints.
Note that the feature is available to the Neon Scale plans only. Details: https://neon.tech/docs/manage/projects#configure-ip-allow
- `allowed_ips_protected_branches_only` (String) Set to 'yes' to activate, 'no' to deactivate explicitly, and omit to keep the default value.
Apply the allow-list to the protected branches only.
Note that the feature is available to the Neon Scale plans only.
- `autoscaling_limit_max_cu` (Number) Maximal value of the project-wide autoscaling limit. 
Note that it is not retrospectively applicable, i.e., existing compute resources are not affected by this configuration.
- `autoscaling_limit_min_cu` (Number) Minimal value of the project-wide autoscaling limit. 
Note that it is not retrospectively applicable, i.e., existing compute resources are not affected by this configuration.
- `block_public_connections` (String) Set to 'yes' to activate, 'no' to deactivate explicitly, and omit to keep the default value.
Block connections from public internet. This supersedes the AllowedIPs list.
- `block_vpc_connections` (String) Set to 'yes' to activate, 'no' to deactivate explicitly, and omit to keep the default value.
Block connections that use VPC endpoints.
- `branch` (Block List, Max: 1) (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--branch))
- `compute_provisioner` (String) Provisioner The Neon compute provisioner.
Specify the k8s-neonvm provisioner to create a compute endpoint that supports Autoscaling.
- `default_branch_protected` (Boolean) Set default branch as protected. **Note** that the default value is false.
- `enable_logical_replication` (String) Set to 'yes' to activate, 'no' to deactivate explicitly, and omit to keep the default value.
Sets wal_level=logical for all compute endpoints in this project.
All active endpoints will be suspended. See details: https://neon.tech/docs/introduction/logical-replication
**Note**: removal of this config from the manifest will correspond to the API call with the respective setting set to false. 

**Warning**: Once enabled, logical replication cannot be disabled.
- `hipaa` (String) Set to 'yes' to activate, 'no' to deactivate explicitly, and omit to keep the default value.
Enable HIPAA compliance for the project. 
Note that HIPAA must be configured for the organization first.

**Warning**: Once enabled, HIPAA cannot be disabled.
- `history_retention_seconds` (Number) The number of seconds to retain the point-in-time restore (PITR) backup history for this project.
Default: 1 day, see https://neon.tech/docs/reference/glossary#point-in-time-restore.
- `maintenance_window` (Block List, Max: 1) A time period during which Neon may perform maintenance on the project's infrastructure. During this time, the project's compute endpoints may be unavailable and existing connections can be interrupted. (see [below for nested schema](#nestedblock--maintenance_window))
- `name` (String) Project name.
- `org_id` (String) Identifier of the organisation to which this project belongs.

entries.name: Monitor
entries.description:
Start a background monitor that streams events from a long-running script. Each stdout line is an event — you keep working and notifications arrive in the chat. Events arrive on their own schedule and are not replies from the user, even if one lands while you're waiting for the user to answer a question.

Pick by how many notifications you need:
- **One** ("tell me when the server is ready / the build finishes") → use **Bash with `run_in_background`** and a command that exits when the condition is true, e.g. `until grep -q "Ready in" dev.log; do sleep 0.5; done`. You get a single completion notification when it exits.
- **One per occurrence, until the monitor expires (re-arm to continue)** ("tell me every time an ERROR line appears") → Monitor with an unbounded command (`tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, `while true`).
- **One per occurrence, until a known end** ("emit each CI step result, stop when the run completes") → Monitor with a command that emits lines and then exits.

Your script's stdout is the event stream. Each line becomes a notification. Exit ends the watch.

  # Each matching log line is an event
  tail -f /var/log/app.log | grep --line-buffered "ERROR"

  # Each file change is an event
  inotifywait -m --format '%e %f' /watched/dir

  # Poll GitHub for new PR comments and emit one line per new comment
  last=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
  while true; do
    now=$(date -u +%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%SZ)
    gh api "repos/owner/repo/issues/123/comments?since=$last" --jq '.[] | "\(.user.login): \(.body)"'
    last=$now; sleep 30
  done

  # Node script that emits events as they arrive (e.g. WebSocket listener)
  node watch-for-events.js

  # Per-occurrence with a natural end: emit each CI check as it lands, exit when the run completes
  prev=""
  while true; do
    s=$(gh pr checks 123 --json name,bucket)
    cur=$(jq -r '.[] | select(.bucket!="pending") | "\(.name): \(.bucket)"' <<<"$s" | sort)
    comm -13 <(echo "$prev") <(echo "$cur")
    prev=$cur
    jq -e 'all(.bucket!="pending")' <<<"$s" >/dev/null && break
    sleep 30
  done

**Don't use an unbounded command for a single notification.** `tail -f`, `inotifywait -m`, and `while true` never exit on their own, so the monitor stays armed until timeout even after the event has fired. For "tell me when X is ready," use Bash `run_in_background` with an `until` loop instead (one notification, ends in seconds). Note that `tail -f log | grep -m 1 ...` does *not* fix this: if the log goes quiet after the match, `tail` never receives SIGPIPE and the pipeline hangs anyway.

**Script quality:**
- Every pipe stage must flush per line or matches sit in its buffer unseen: `grep` needs `--line-buffered`, `awk` needs `fflush()`. `head` cannot flush at all — `| head -N` delivers nothing until N matches accumulate, then ends the stream.
- In poll loops, handle transient failures (`curl ... || true`) — one failed request shouldn't kill the monitor.
- Poll intervals: 30s+ for remote APIs (rate limits), 0.5-1s for local checks.
- Write a specific `description` — it appears in every notification ("errors in deploy.log" not "watching logs").
- Only stdout is the event stream. Stderr goes to the output file (readable via Read) but does not trigger notifications — for a command you run directly (e.g. `python train.py 2>&1 | grep --line-buffered ...`), merge stderr with `2>&1` so its failures reach your filter. (No effect on `tail -f` of an existing log — that file only contains what its writer redirected.)

**Coverage — silence is not success.** When watching a job or process for an outcome, your filter must match every terminal state, not just the happy path. A monitor that greps only for the success marker stays silent through a crashloop, a hung process, or an unexpected exit — and silence looks identical to "still running." Before arming, ask: *if this process crashed right now, would my filter emit anything?* If not, widen it.

  # Wrong — silent on crash, hang, or any non-success exit
  tail -f run.log | grep --line-buffered "elapsed_steps="

  # Right — one alternation covering progress + the failure signatures you'd act on
  tail -f run.log | grep -E --line-buffered "elapsed_steps=|Traceback|Error|FAILED|assert|Killed|OOM"

For poll loops checking job state, emit on every terminal status (`succeeded|failed|cancelled|timeout`), not just success. If you cannot confidently enumerate the failure signatures, broaden the grep alternation rather than narrow it — some extra noise is better than missing a crashloop.

**Output volume**: Every stdout line is a conversation message, so the filter should be selective — but selective means "the lines you'd act on," not "only good news." Never pipe raw logs; filter to exactly the success and failure signals you care about. Monitors that produce too many events are automatically stopped; restart with a tighter filter if this happens.

Stdout lines within 200ms are batched into a single notification, so multiline output from a single event groups naturally.

The script runs in the same shell environment as Bash. Exit ends the watch (exit code is reported). Every monitor expires after `timeout_ms` (default 5 minutes, at most 30 minutes): it is killed and you get one notice with the event count. Re-arm it if you still need the watch; for a long watch (PR monitoring, log tails) set `timeout_ms` to the maximum and re-arm on each expiry, and widen the filter if an expiry with no events was unexpected. Use TaskStop to cancel early.
**ws source** — open a WebSocket and stream each incoming text frame as an event. No shell, no polling: the server pushes, you get notified.

  Monitor({
    ws: {url: 'wss://events.example.com/stream', protocols: ['v1']},
    description: 'deploy events',
  })

Each text frame becomes one notification (multiline frames stay as one event). Binary frames are reported as `[binary frame, N bytes]` rather than passed through. Socket close ends the watch with the close code surfaced; errors are surfaced before close. Same rate limiting as bash — a firehose will be suppressed and eventually stopped, so subscribe to a filtered feed where one exists.

Prefer this over `command: 'websocat wss://…'` — it avoids the extra process and line-buffering pitfalls. Use bash when you need to transform or filter frames with shell tools before they become events.

description.description: Short human-readable description of what you are monitoring (shown in notifications).

timeout_ms.description: Kill the monitor after this deadline. Default 300000ms. Deadlines above 1800000ms are capped to 1800000ms. You are notified at expiry and can re-arm.

command.description: Shell command or script. Each stdout line is an event; exit ends the watch.

ws.description: WebSocket to open. Each text frame is an event; binary frames are reported as a placeholder line. Socket close ends the watch. Cannot be combined with command.

Based on the search results, here's the information about Lambda Function URL resource policies with AUTH_TYPE NONE:

## Key Requirements

If you choose the NONE auth type, Lambda doesn't use IAM to authenticate requests to your function URL. However, your function must have a resource-based policy that allows lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction.

## Permission Requirements

To invoke a function URL, you must have lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions. When you use the AWS CLI, you must add the lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction statements separately.

## Recent Changes (2025)

Starting in October 2025, new function URLs will require both lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl and lambda:InvokeFunction permissions.

## Resource Policy Structure

When your function URL auth type is NONE and you have a resource-based policy that grants public access, any unauthenticated user with your function URL can invoke your function.

The search results indicate that even with AUTH_TYPE set to NONE, both the `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` and `lambda:InvokeFunction` actions must be explicitly granted in the resource-based policy to allow invocations.

## Key Points

The `function_url_auth_type` parameter is optional and accepts valid values of `AWS_IAM` or `NONE`. It is only supported for the `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` action.

## Two Permissions Pattern

When using `function_url_auth_type` set to `NONE`, you must add the resource-based policy yourself using separate statements for both the `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` and `lambda:InvokeFunction` permissions, with each statement added in a separate command.

## Example Configuration

An example shows using `aws_lambda_permission` with `action = "lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl"`, `principal = "*"`, and `function_url_auth_type = "NONE"`. 

Additionally, AWS documentation shows adding permissions for both `lambda:InvokeFunctionUrl` with `function-url-auth-type NONE` and `lambda:InvokeFunction` with the `invoked-via-function-url` flag.

This dual-permission approach ensures proper access control when publicly exposing a Lambda function URL without IAM authentication.
